patient.chief_complaint: Progressive gait deterioration, urinary urgency, and cognitive slowing — admitted for neurological workup after prior spine workup was inconclusive
patient.history_present_illness: A 72-year-old right-handed retired mechanical engineer with degenerative lumbar spine disease, hypertension, and hyperlipidemia was admitted for comprehensive neurological evaluation of a 20-month history of progressive gait deterioration, cognitive slowing, and urinary urgency. The gait problem was first noticed approximately 20 months ago. His wife described him as beginning to 'shuffle and drag his feet,' with difficulty lifting his feet off the floor. He was seen by his primary care physician, who — noting a prior lumbar MRI showing moderate L4-L5 central canal stenosis — attributed the gait to neurogenic claudication from lumbar spinal stenosis and referred him to orthopedic spine surgery. He underwent extensive spine evaluation over the following months including a repeat lumbar MRI and electromyography (reported as mild L4-L5 radiculopathy). Orthopedic surgery recommended lumbar decompression (L3-L5 laminectomy), but the procedure was deferred after the patient and his wife felt his gait did not improve with a trial of epidural steroid injections and expressed concerns about surgery. His wife noted two features that the spine team had not focused on: (1) the gait appeared 'magnetic' — he seemed unable to lift his feet from the floor even when standing still on a flat surface with no exertion, very different from the 'cramping and stopping after walking' she had read about with spinal stenosis; and (2) urinary urgency with two to three accidents per week had begun approximately 14 months ago. Over the past year the patient has also developed noticeable cognitive slowing — he takes longer to follow conversations, has difficulty planning tasks he previously performed independently, and repeats questions within the same hour. His wife brought him to his internist who was struck by the cognitive findings, ordered a head CT that showed enlarged ventricles, and referred him urgently to neurology. He was admitted for brain MRI and tap-trial evaluation. He has had no headaches, no nausea, no papilledema, and no history of prior head trauma, meningitis, or subarachnoid hemorrhage. He has not noticed any leg weakness, dermatomal pain radiating down the leg, or pain that worsens with standing and improves with leaning forward or sitting (classic neurogenic claudication pattern).

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert and oriented to person, place, and date. MoCA 21/30 (loses 4 points on delayed recall, 2 on Trail-Making/abstraction, 3 on visuospatial/executive). MMSE 25/30. Speech is fluent but mildly slowed in rate. No aphasia. No agnosia. Patient is aware of his memory difficulty.
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal, round, and reactive to light, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements full without restriction or nystagmus. Facial sensation intact and symmetric. Tongue midline. Hearing intact to finger rub bilaterally. No papilledema on fundoscopic examination.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal bulk and tone bilaterally. No cogwheel rigidity. No resting tremor. Strength 5/5 in all four limbs including hip flexors, knee extensors, ankle dorsiflexors, and plantar flexors. No fasciculations. Mild bilateral lower extremity tone increase difficult to characterize.
neurological_exam.sensory: Light touch intact bilaterally. Pinprick intact bilaterally including L4 and L5 dermatomes. Vibration mildly reduced at the great toes bilaterally (age-appropriate). Proprioception intact at the ankles bilaterally. No Lhermitte sign. No dermatomal sensory loss.
neurological_exam.reflexes: Biceps 2+ bilaterally. Triceps 2+ bilaterally. Brachioradialis 2+ bilaterally. Patellar 2+ bilaterally. Achilles 1+ bilaterally. Plantar responses flexor bilaterally. No ankle clonus. No Babinski sign.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-shin intact bilaterally. Rapid alternating movements mildly slow but symmetric.
neurological_exam.gait: Wide-based, magnetic gait with markedly reduced step height — feet barely clear the floor on flat surface. Short steps, reduced arm swing bilaterally. Freezing at initiation ('start hesitation') lasting 3-4 seconds. Slow cadence. Requires multiple small steps to turn around. Unable to tandem walk. TUG (Timed Up and Go): 28 seconds. 10-meter walk: 22 seconds. Gait does not worsen significantly with prolonged walking, and the patient does not stop or describe cramping in the legs with exertion. Pull test: 2-3 steps backward, does not fall.
neurological_exam.additional: No cogwheel or lead-pipe rigidity. No resting or postural tremor. Bilateral grasp reflexes present. Snout reflex present. No nuchal rigidity. No Romberg sign.

findings.location: bilateral lateral ventricles and third ventricle

signal_characteristics.description: Evans index 0.35. Marked enlargement of bilateral lateral ventricles and third ventricle disproportionate to degree of cortical atrophy. Cortical sulci at vertex and high convexity are effaced. Sylvian fissures are widened bilaterally.

Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid space hydrocephalus (DESH) pattern: tight sulci at high convexity bilaterally with relatively widened Sylvian fissures. High-convexity sulcal effacement evident on axial and coronal sequences.

findings.location: corpus callosum — coronal plane at posterior commissure

signal_characteristics.description: Callosal angle 72 degrees on coronal FLAIR (reference: <90 degrees supports NPH pattern).
Smooth periventricular FLAIR halos (transependymal CSF signal) bilaterally. Moderate subcortical white matter FLAIR hyperintensity (Fazekas grade 2).
Prominent T2 flow void in the aqueduct of Sylvius consistent with hyperdynamic CSF pulsatility.

Posterior fossa structures normal. No mass, enhancing lesion, or structural obstruction at the aqueduct or foramen of Monro. No prior hemorrhagic signal. No sulcal FLAIR signal (no leptomeningeal disease). Hippocampal volumes mildly reduced bilaterally for age but not disproportionately atrophied.

additional_observations: Comparison with lumbar spine MRI performed 14 months ago is not applicable (different study). No prior brain MRI available for comparison.

Lumbar spine MRI from 14 months ago (external study, reviewed on disc): L4-L5 moderate central canal stenosis with ligamentum flavum hypertrophy and disc-osteophyte complex. L3-L4 mild foraminal narrowing. Those findings are a lumbar-spine-level study and are not assessed on the current brain MRI.
mri.impression: 1. Ventriculomegaly with Evans index 0.35 and callosal angle 72°. DESH pattern: tight high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures. Prominent aqueductal CSF flow void. Periventricular transependymal signal. These findings are consistent with communicating hydrocephalus in an appropriate clinical context. 2. Moderate subcortical white matter FLAIR hyperintensity (Fazekas grade 2), consistent with small vessel ischemic disease. 3. No mass, enhancing lesion, hemorrhage, or structural aqueductal obstruction. 4. Mild bilateral hippocampal volume reduction for age

labs.interpretation: All values within normal limits. TSH, vitamin B12, RPR, and HIV screening non-reactive.

special_tests.gait_observation_post_tap: Step height visibly increased at 24-hour assessment; start hesitation absent; turned in fewer steps

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 17 cmH2O (normal). WBC: 1 cell/mcL. Protein: 46 mg/dL. Glucose: 64 mg/dL (ratio 0.66). No organisms on Gram stain. No malignant cells on cytology. TUG improved from 28 seconds pre-tap to 19 seconds at 24 hours (32% improvement). 10-meter walk improved from 22 seconds to 15 seconds at 24 hours (32% improvement). MoCA improved from 21 to 23 at 24 hours

Predominant deficits in executive function and processing speed, with mild episodic memory impairment. Memory encoding failure is not disproportionate and recognition is intact. inph_vs_lumbar_spinal_stenosis.query: iNPH gait versus neurogenic claudication lumbar spinal stenosis differential diagnosis magnetic gait

results.title: Distinguishing iNPH gait from neurogenic claudication: clinical and biomechanical features
results.key_finding: Magnetic/apraxic gait in iNPH is present at rest and on flat surfaces without exertion; neurogenic claudication worsens with prolonged walking or standing and improves with flexion or sitting. Wide base, reduced step height, and start hesitation are more characteristic of iNPH. Clinical examination and brain MRI Evans index >0.3 with DESH confirm iNPH.

results.title: Normal pressure hydrocephalus misdiagnosed as lumbar spinal stenosis — a common clinical pitfall
results.key_finding: A significant proportion of patients with iNPH who undergo lumbar spine surgery for presumed neurogenic claudication have unrecognized comorbid ventriculomegaly. Concurrent lumbar canal stenosis on MRI does not exclude iNPH and may coexist; brain MRI with Evans index and callosal angle measurement is recommended in all patients with gait disorders before attributing symptoms solely to a spinal cause.

results.title: Relkin N et al. Diagnosing idiopathic normal-pressure hydrocephalus. Neurosurgery 2005
results.key_finding: Probable iNPH requires Hakim's triad, Evans index >0.3, chronic course, normal opening pressure <25 cmH2O, and absence of an alternative explanatory condition. Lumbar canal stenosis is not an exclusion criterion if gait characteristics and brain MRI satisfy NPH criteria. Tap test response (30-50 mL LP) with pre/post objective gait assessment is the key predictive test for shunt responsiveness.

inph_vs_lumbar_spinal_stenosis.summary: In patients presenting with gait disorder and known lumbar spine disease, iNPH and neurogenic claudication can coexist or be confused. Key distinguishing features: iNPH gait is magnetic/apraxic (present at rest, no claudicant component), wide-based, with start hesitation; neurogenic claudication is exertion- and position-dependent. Brain MRI showing Evans index >0.3 with DESH pattern and callosal angle <90° in a patient with Hakim's triad warrants tap-test evaluation regardless of lumbar spine findings. [Relkin_2005]

differential.key_features: Documented L4-L5 central canal stenosis on prior lumbar MRI anchors early diagnostic thinking, but gait is magnetic/apraxic (present at rest, no claudicant exertion-dependence), brain MRI shows DESH with Evans index 0.35, and triad includes cognitive slowing and urinary urgency — findings not explained by lumbar stenosis alone

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Moderate white matter disease (Fazekas 2) could contribute to gait and cognition, but ventriculomegaly disproportionate to white-matter burden, DESH pattern, callosal angle 72°, and positive tap test favour NPH
Shuffling gait with reduced arm swing overlaps, but absence of resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, or asymmetric onset, and presence of wide-based magnetic gait with DESH, favour iNPH over PD

Cognitive slowing is present but frontal-subcortical in pattern with intact recognition memory; CSF AD biomarkers normal; amyloid PET negative; hippocampal atrophy only mild; gait disturbance markedly disproportionate to cognitive deficit

No cervical MRI obtained but exam lacks upper motor neuron signs (Babinski absent, no hyperreflexia, no Lhermitte), no hand clumsiness or grip weakness, and broad-based magnetic gait without spastic component argues against cervical cord compression as the primary cause

optimal_actions.expected_finding: Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group criteria; gait distinctions between iNPH (magnetic, present at rest) and neurogenic claudication (exertion- and position-dependent); concurrent lumbar stenosis does not exclude iNPH

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI (cranial, not lumbar) — measure Evans index, callosal angle, assess DESH pattern; this is the key study that reframes the spine-anchored diagnostic picture
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Evans index 0.35, callosal angle 72°, DESH (tight high-convexity sulci + widened Sylvian fissures), periventricular transependymal signal, prominent aqueductal flow void; no mass effect or obstructive lesion

optimal_actions.action: Reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) to exclude metabolic and infectious dementia mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: TSH, B12, RPR, HIV all within normal limits; reversible mimics excluded

optimal_actions.action: Baseline neuropsychological battery — characterise pattern (frontal-subcortical vs amnestic) and establish pre-tap reference for post-tap comparison
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Frontal-subcortical pattern: executive dysfunction and processing speed impairment predominate; episodic memory mildly impaired with intact recognition; not a primary amnestic AD profile

optimal_actions.action: Large-volume lumbar puncture (40 mL tap test) with opening pressure measurement and pre/post objective gait and cognitive assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Opening pressure 17 cmH2O (normal <25); 40 mL removed; TUG improves 32% at 24 hours; 10-m walk improves 32%; MoCA improves 2 points; CSF biomarkers normal

optimal_actions.action: Neurosurgery consultation for VP shunt candidacy evaluation
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Neurosurgery accepts patient for VP shunt placement with programmable valve given positive imaging, normal opening pressure, and positive tap trial

optimal_actions.action: Amyloid PET (optional) — screen for AD copathology that may temper cognitive but not gait shunt benefit
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Negative amyloid PET (CL score 18) — no significant AD copathology in this case

optimal_actions.action: Measure gait and balance objectively before the large-volume tap — timed-up-and-go, 10-metre walk, step length, falls risk — and repeat the same measures and the cognitive screen after it. The baseline must be recorded before the puncture or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Baseline timed gait recorded before the tap and repeated after it, with the response read against the >=20% threshold and the cognitive screen repeated alongside

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific for iNPH and does not differentiate it from neurodegenerative alternatives in this chronic gait/cognitive/urinary triad presentation
ECG does not contribute to the NPH diagnostic workup; cardiogenic syncope and arrhythmia are not on the differential
Echocardiography is not indicated in the NPH evaluation in the absence of syncope or suspected cardioembolic stroke workup
Head CT is inferior to brain MRI for measuring Evans index, callosal angle, and DESH pattern; justified only if MRI is contraindicated
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in the iNPH workup; not indicated without syncope or palpitations

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain MRI must precede large-volume LP to exclude mass effect, obstructive hydrocephalus, or structural aqueductal lesion before removing 40 mL of CSF
The baseline gait and cognition must be measured before the large-volume tap, or the post-tap change cannot be interpreted and the tap test yields nothing

critical_actions: Obtain cranial brain MRI (not lumbar spine MRI) as the key reframing study — measure Evans index, callosal angle, and DESH pattern to establish whether ventriculomegaly satisfies iNPH imaging criteria

Distinguish magnetic/apraxic gait from neurogenic claudication: magnetic gait is present at rest and on flat surfaces without exertion and does not improve with leaning forward or sitting; neurogenic claudication is exertion- and position-dependent
Perform large-volume tap test (30-50 mL) with objective pre/post gait assessment (TUG, 10-metre walk) and cognitive reassessment at 1-4 hours and 24 hours post-tap
Obtain reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) before attributing the triad to iNPH
Establish baseline neuropsychological profile before tap test to quantify post-tap cognitive change
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt evaluation when imaging, clinical triad, and tap-test response criteria are met
contraindicated_actions: Do not proceed to lumbar decompression surgery for a gait that is magnetic/apraxic in character — the gait of iNPH is not explained by lumbar canal stenosis and will not respond to spinal decompression

Do not attribute the full clinical syndrome (magnetic gait + urinary urgency + cognitive slowing + ventriculomegaly with DESH) to lumbar spinal stenosis; spine disease is a comorbidity, not a sufficient explanation
Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before cranial brain MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not infer iNPH from ventriculomegaly alone — DESH pattern, callosal angle <90°, and the full clinical triad are required
Do not diagnose Alzheimer's disease in a patient with gait-predominant presentation and ventriculomegaly without first excluding iNPH
key_reasoning_points: Lumbar spinal stenosis is the most common misdiagnosis in this case: documented L4-L5 central canal stenosis on lumbar MRI anchors early diagnostic thinking toward neurogenic claudication, but the gait character is magnetic and apraxic (feet barely clear flat floor even at rest, start hesitation, wide base) — not the exertion-dependent cramping with relief on sitting that defines neurogenic claudication

Neurogenic claudication from lumbar stenosis does not cause urinary urgency or cognitive slowing in the absence of spinal cord compression — the full Hakim's triad directs attention to a central, not spinal, cause

The cranial brain MRI is the pivotal reframing study: Evans index 0.35, callosal angle 72°, DESH pattern (tight high-convexity sulci + widened Sylvian fissures), and periventricular transependymal signal all support communicating hydrocephalus in the NPH pattern — findings entirely absent on any lumbar spine study

Concurrent lumbar canal stenosis does not exclude iNPH and commonly coexists in older patients; the two conditions require separate evaluation and the presence of one does not confirm or exclude the other

The tap test result (32% TUG and 10-m walk improvement at 24 hours after 40 mL removal, opening pressure 17 cmH2O) satisfies the Relkin 2005 criteria for probable iNPH with positive tap response and predicts shunt responsiveness

The neuropsychological profile is frontal-subcortical (executive and processing speed predominant, intact recognition memory) — not the amnestic hippocampal profile of AD — consistent with iNPH and distinguishable from primary dementia syndromes
Tier per the July 2026 clinical review: The reversible-cause screen is good practice but does not establish or exclude hydrocephalus; the tap test does.

red_herrings.data_point: L4-L5 moderate central canal stenosis on lumbar MRI (obtained 14 months prior) with subsequent spine surgery evaluation and epidural steroid injections
red_herrings.intended_effect: The documented lumbar canal stenosis anchors diagnostic thinking toward neurogenic claudication as the explanation for gait deterioration, causing the clinician to pursue lumbar decompression and delay brain MRI and iNPH workup
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: Lumbar canal stenosis is a genuine but non-explanatory comorbidity: the gait is magnetic/apraxic (present at rest, no exertion-dependence, no claudicant pattern), and the full triad with ventriculomegaly/DESH/callosal angle 72° identifies iNPH as the primary diagnosis; spinal decompression would not address the hydrocephalic gait

red_herrings.data_point: Gait initially described to the spine team as worsening with prolonged ambulation — consistent with the spine history — but neurological exam demonstrates magnetic/apraxic character (feet barely clear flat surface at rest, start hesitation, no position-related improvement)
red_herrings.intended_effect: The history of gait worsening with ambulation, in the context of known lumbar stenosis, is read as confirming neurogenic claudication, perpetuating the spine-anchored diagnosis
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The neurological examination distinguishes the gait type: magnetic gait with start hesitation and inability to lift feet even at rest on a flat surface is not neurogenic claudication; objective TUG/10-m walk and response to tap test confirm the hydrocephalic gait etiology

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Moderate iNPH in a 72-year-old retired engineer — gait extensively misattributed to lumbar spinal stenosis (documented L4-L5 central canal stenosis, spine surgery evaluation, epidural steroid injections) before full triad and cranial ventriculomegaly/DESH recognised. First spine-misattribution NPH case in the dataset. Tests agent ability to distinguish magnetic gait from neurogenic claudication and to request cranial MRI despite established spine diagnosis.
metadata.revision_reason: July 2026 clinical tool review, per-annotation closure: order_specialized_test required -> optional: the mandatory objective assessment is perform_clinical_assessment{gait_and_balance_timed}, which carries the pre/post tap comparison; the standalone battery is the duplication the review asked to remove; dropped the redundant order_specialized_test -> analyze_csf constraint; the identical rule on perform_clinical_assessment carries it
metadata.difficulty_rationale: 5 required tools (cranial MRI, labs, neuropsych baseline, large-volume LP/tap, literature) + 1 recommended (neurosurgery consult); 2 grounded red herrings (lumbar MRI stenosis, gait-as-claudication misread); differential includes lumbar spinal stenosis as the high-likelihood alternative requiring active rule-out; requires cross-modality synthesis (spine history vs cranial imaging vs gait exam vs tap response) and explicit gait-type discrimination
